Accurate time matters far beyond appearances: logs from several devices can only be correlated if their timestamps agree, and certificates and authentication tokens depend on a correct clock.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to NAT and DHCP? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A large office building has hundreds of staff with internal extension numbers, but only one public phone number. The switchboard operator (PAT) writes down which internal extension made each outside call, and when the reply arrives she connects it back to the right desk, so everyone shares one public number. A static mapping is a direct dial number given to one person so customers can call them anytime. DHCP is the receptionist who hands every newcomer a desk number, the phone book (DNS) and the building clock (NTP). The helper-address is the hotel porter who carries a new arrival's request to the reception desk on another floor.
commonTraps: Reading the NAT table backwards: the inside local column is the private address, the inside global column is the translated one.
Thinking the NAT ACL permits or denies traffic; it only decides what is translated.
Putting ip helper-address on the server-facing interface instead of the client-facing one.
Confusing static NAT, which allows inbound sessions, with dynamic NAT and PAT, which create entries only for outbound flows.
Counting stratum wrongly: each downstream device is one higher than its source, and 16 means not synchronized.
lessons.scenario: A branch office of 80 users has one public address from its ISP. The engineer enables ip nat inside on the LAN interface and ip nat outside on the WAN interface, writes access-list 1 permit 10.20.0.0 0.0.0.255 and enters ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload. A web server at 10.20.0.10 is published with ip nat inside source static 10.20.0.10 203.0.113.10. DHCP clients in a second VLAN get addresses through ip helper-address on the VLAN gateway interface, and the router synchronizes its clock with ntp server 203.0.113.50 so that logs line up with headquarters.
lessons.onTheJob: Most NAT problems come from three places: an interface missing its inside or outside marking, an ACL that does not match the real inside subnet, or asymmetric routing that sends the reply around the translating router. Learn to read show ip nat translations column by column, and use clear ip nat translation * to force fresh entries when testing. Exclude addresses of gateways, printers and servers from every DHCP pool before enabling it, and use short leases on guest networks. Point all devices to the same trusted NTP sources before an incident, not during one; mismatched clocks make post-incident analysis miserable and can break certificate validation.

lessons.title: SNMP, Syslog, QoS, SSH and File Transfer
lessons.summary: The management and quality services of an IP network: monitoring with SNMP, logging with syslog, prioritizing traffic with QoS, secure remote access with SSH and moving files with TFTP and FTP.
lessons.reading:
Networks need to be watched, remembered and kept fair. SNMP covers watching. A network management station polls an SNMP agent on each device, typically on UDP 161, for variables defined in the management information base, each identified by an object identifier. The agent can also volunteer an alert, a trap, to the station on UDP 162; an inform is a trap the manager must acknowledge, so it is resent if lost. SNMPv1 and v2c authenticate with a community string sent in clear text, so treat them as unsafe on untrusted paths. SNMPv3 adds named users, authentication and optional encryption, and authPriv, which does both, is the secure answer on the exam.

Syslog covers remembering. Devices send log messages, by default over UDP 514, to a collector configured with logging host. Every message carries a severity from 0 to 7: Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notice, Informational, Debugging. A lower number is more severe, and setting a threshold sends that level and everything more severe, so logging trap 4 forwards levels 0 to 4 and discards Notice, Informational and Debugging. The console and buffer have their own thresholds, and service timestamps give each message a time that is only trustworthy if NTP is working.

QoS keeps priority traffic usable when links are congested. It works in steps. Classification identifies the traffic, for example with an ACL or by application. Marking writes the result into the packet: CoS in the 802.1Q tag at Layer 2 and DSCP in the IP header at Layer 3, ideally set at the trust boundary near the source. Queuing and scheduling then decide what leaves first when the interface is busy. FIFO treats all traffic alike; class-based weighted fair queuing guarantees shares; low-latency queuing adds a strict priority queue for voice, usually marked EF (DSCP 46), whose requirements are tight: roughly 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter and under 1 percent loss. Weighted random early detection drops lower-priority packets early to avoid tail drop. Policing drops or remarks traffic above a rate and never buffers it, while shaping buffers the excess and sends it later at the contracted rate, trading delay for fewer drops.

SSH replaces Telnet for remote CLI access, because it encrypts the whole session including the password. To enable it on a Cisco device you need a hostname and a domain name, an RSA key pair (crypto key generate rsa), a local user, and vty lines set with login local and transport input ssh; ip ssh version 2 requires the stronger protocol version. If the key generation complains about a missing domain name, the domain name comes first.

For moving files, TFTP (UDP 69) is simple and unauthenticated, handy in a lab for copying configurations and IOS images, and FTP (TCP 21 plus a data connection) adds credentials but still sends them in clear text. SCP and SFTP, which ride on SSH, are the secure choices. The CCNA expects you to pick between these by their characteristics: no authentication and UDP means TFTP, credentials and TCP means FTP.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to network management? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of running a hospital ward. SNMP is the nurse who walks round with a clipboard reading each patient's temperature, and a trap is a patient pressing the call button. Syslog is the patient notes file: every event is written down with a severity, and the most urgent entries (a cardiac arrest, level 0) are the ones that page the doctor. QoS is the triage desk deciding that an emergency case goes ahead of a routine check-up, even when the waiting room is full, and policing and shaping are the difference between turning extra patients away and asking them to wait. SSH is the locked door to the staff room, and TFTP is passing a file across the counter with no ID check.
commonTraps: Mixing up syslog severity direction: level 0 is the most severe, and a threshold includes all more severe levels.
Believing SNMPv2c is secure because the community string looks like a password; it travels in clear text.
Confusing policing (drops or remarks, no buffer) with shaping (buffers and delays).
Forgetting that SSH needs a domain name before an RSA key can be generated, and that login local plus transport input ssh finish the job.
Assuming TFTP or FTP is secure; neither encrypts, so the secure options are SCP and SFTP.
lessons.scenario: A retailer's head office monitors 200 branch routers. The engineer configures SNMPv3 users with authPriv, sends syslog messages at level warnings and above to a central collector, and marks voice traffic EF at the access switches. On each WAN router, low-latency queuing gives voice a strict priority queue, and a shaper limits traffic to the 20 Mbps contracted rate so the provider does not discard bursts. Administrators reach the routers only through SSH on lines configured with login local and transport input ssh, and use SCP to load new software images.
lessons.onTheJob: Do not leave a read-write SNMP community string at a default value such as private; attackers scan for it. Choose syslog levels deliberately: logging at debugging level to the console of a busy router can degrade it. QoS has to be consistent end to end, so agree on a marking scheme and a trust boundary before touching a single policy map, because a policy on one device means little if the next hop re-marks everything to zero. Verify queue behavior under real load, not on an idle link, since QoS only matters when there is congestion. Retire Telnet and plain FTP everywhere you can, and keep SSH keys at 2048 bits or larger.

lessons.title: Security Concepts, Device Hardening, AAA and VPNs
lessons.summary: Threats, vulnerabilities and attacks; the elements of a security program; hardening device access with local passwords; AAA with RADIUS and TACACS+; and site-to-site versus remote-access VPNs.
lessons.reading:
Security starts with vocabulary. An asset is something worth protecting. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as an unpatched operating system or a default password. A threat is something that could exploit it, an exploit is the code or technique that actually does, and risk is the likelihood and impact of that happening. Controls that reduce risk are called mitigations. The CIA triad names the goals: confidentiality (only the right people see data), integrity (data cannot be changed unnoticed) and availability (systems work when needed).

You should recognise the common attacks. A denial-of-service attack floods or crashes a target, and a distributed version uses many hosts at once. Spoofing forges an address or identity, and reflection and amplification abuse third-party servers to flood a victim. A man-in-the-middle attacker relays and may alter traffic, for example after ARP poisoning. Malware includes viruses that need a host action, worms that spread alone across the network, trojans that disguise themselves and ransomware that encrypts data for payment. Social engineering attacks the person: phishing is a broad fraudulent message, spear phishing is aimed at one individual, and vishing uses a phone call.

Technology alone cannot cover these threats, so a security program combines user awareness (people know threats exist), user training (people know what to do) and physical access control (locks, badges, cameras), because an intruder who can plug into a switch or reset a router bypasses every software control. A password policy sets minimum length, complexity and reuse rules, and encourages multifactor authentication, which combines different factor types: something you know, something you have and something you are.

On Cisco devices, local access control starts with enable secret for privileged EXEC, stored as a one-way salted hash (type 9, scrypt, is the strongest). Line passwords or, better, local usernames with login local protect the console and vty lines, exec-timeout closes idle sessions and login block-for slows brute-force attempts. service password-encryption only obfuscates plain passwords with the reversible type 7 scheme; it is no substitute for a secret. Central control scales better: AAA separates authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do) and accounting (what did you do). RADIUS is an open standard on UDP that combines authentication and authorization and encrypts only the password; TACACS+ is Cisco-originated on TCP 49, separates all three functions and encrypts the entire payload, so it is preferred for device administration with per-command authorization.

VPNs protect traffic across untrusted networks. A site-to-site VPN, normally IPsec between two routers or firewalls, joins whole networks and is invisible to the hosts. A remote-access VPN connects one user's device on demand, using client software with IPsec or SSL/TLS, and authenticates the user. IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication using ESP after IKE negotiation, while GRE is a tunnelling protocol that carries other protocols and multicast but offers no encryption, so GRE over IPsec is used when routing protocols must cross an encrypted tunnel.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security terminology? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a shop. The unlocked back door is the vulnerability, a burglar is the threat, and the crowbar or a copied key is the exploit. Risk is how likely a burglary is multiplied by what you would lose. Mitigations are the lock, the alarm, the camera and staff who know not to hand the keys to a stranger in a hi-vis jacket, which is social engineering. AAA is the staff room: the badge scanner proves who you are, the rota decides which rooms you may enter, and the logbook records when you went in. A VPN is an armoured van that carries the day's takings between two shops, or a locked briefcase for the manager travelling home.
commonTraps: Mixing up threat, vulnerability and exploit; the weakness is the vulnerability, the code that abuses it is the exploit.
Treating service password-encryption as strong security; type 7 is reversible, and enable secret is what to rely on.
Choosing RADIUS where per-command authorization is requested; TACACS+ is the one that separates authorization.
Believing GRE encrypts; it needs IPsec for protection.
Calling a mass fraudulent email spear phishing; spear phishing is targeted at one person or small group.
lessons.scenario: A regional bank hardens a new branch router. The engineer sets enable secret with a long passphrase, creates local users with secrets, restricts the vty lines with login local and transport input ssh and adds exec-timeout and login block-for. Network administrators authenticate to a central TACACS+ server, with the local database as fallback, so that junior engineers can run show commands but not change configurations, and every command is accounted for. Branch connectivity to headquarters runs over an IPsec site-to-site VPN, while teleworkers use a remote-access VPN client with multifactor authentication.
lessons.onTheJob: Always configure a local fallback account when you move device logins to AAA, or a server outage will lock you out of the whole network, and test the fallback before you need it. Remember that the bulk of real incidents begin with a person: a convincing email, a reused password or an unattended console. Budget for awareness training and physical access control as seriously as for firewalls. For VPNs, size the router for the encryption workload and remember that a site-to-site tunnel proves nothing about the safety of the machines at each end; combine it with segmentation and filtering.

lessons.title: ACLs, Layer 2 Security and Wireless Security
lessons.summary: Writing and placing standard and extended ACLs with wildcard masks, protecting access ports with port security, DHCP snooping and DAI, and choosing wireless security protocols.
lessons.reading:
An access control list is an ordered list of permit and deny rules that a router applies to packets. A standard ACL (numbers 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999, or a named standard ACL) matches only the source IPv4 address. An extended ACL (100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699, or named) matches protocol, source, destination and, for TCP and UDP, port numbers. Two rules govern every ACL. Entries are checked from top to bottom and the first match decides, so specific entries must come before general ones; and there is an invisible deny any at the very end, so an ACL consisting of only deny lines blocks everything. A line such as permit ip any any placed too early makes all later entries unreachable.

Addresses in ACLs use wildcard masks, the inverse of a subnet mask: a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored. A /24 is 0.0.0.255, a /26 is 0.0.0.63 and a /27 is 0.0.0.31. The shortcut host x.x.x.x means wildcard 0.0.0.0, and any means 255.255.255.255. To find a wildcard, subtract the subnet mask from 255 in each octet. The range 172.16.32.0 to 172.16.47.255 is a /20, so the wildcard is 0.0.15.255. Apply the ACL to an interface with ip access-group name-or-number in or out; you can have one ACL per protocol, per direction, per interface. The classic placement rule is extended ACLs close to the source, so unwanted traffic dies early, and standard ACLs close to the destination, since they cannot say where the traffic is going. An outbound ACL does not filter traffic the router itself originates, and access-class applies an ACL to the vty lines to limit who may manage the device. Named ACLs show sequence numbers, which let you insert a line between existing ones.

Layer 2 needs its own protection because attacks happen before packets ever reach a router. Port security limits the MAC addresses on an access port: by default one address is allowed and the violation mode is shutdown, which puts the port in err-disabled state until you enter shutdown and no shutdown; restrict drops and logs, and protect drops silently. Addresses can be set by hand or learned as sticky entries. DHCP snooping divides ports into trusted (toward the real DHCP server and uplinks) and untrusted (everything else). The switch drops DHCP server messages arriving on untrusted ports, defeating rogue servers, and builds a binding table of MAC, IP, VLAN and port. Dynamic ARP inspection uses that table to check every ARP packet on untrusted ports and drops forged replies, stopping ARP poisoning, so DAI needs snooping and trusted uplinks to work.

Wireless networks broadcast into the air, so the security protocol matters. WEP (RC4) is broken and must not be used. WPA used TKIP as a stopgap. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP: Personal mode shares one passphrase of 8 to 63 ASCII characters, while Enterprise mode authenticates every user with 802.1X and a RADIUS server, so access can be revoked individually. WPA3 improves on WPA2 with SAE in Personal mode, which resists offline dictionary attacks on a captured handshake, mandatory protected management frames and stronger enterprise options. Hiding the SSID or filtering MAC addresses is not real security. On a wireless LAN controller, a WPA2-PSK WLAN is created under WLANs, then the Security tab, Layer 2, WPA+WPA2 with PSK and the passphrase.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to ACLs and Layer 2 security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: An ACL is a security guard with a clipboard who reads the list from the top for every visitor and stops at the first line that matches. If the visitor matches no line, the guard turns them away, because the last line of every list says 'nobody else'. Wildcard masks are the guard's way of saying 'any visitor whose badge starts with these digits'. Port security is a hotel key-card limited to one registered device per room. DHCP snooping makes sure only the front desk, not a stranger in the corridor, hands out room numbers, and DAI checks every 'who lives in room 12?' question against the front desk's register.
commonTraps: Putting a general permit ahead of a specific deny so the deny is never reached.
Forgetting the implicit deny: an ACL with only deny statements blocks every other packet.
Using the block size or a subnet mask instead of the true wildcard (a /27 wildcard is 0.0.0.31, not 0.0.0.32 or 255.255.255.224).
Placing a standard ACL near the source, where it blocks that host from everywhere instead of from one destination.
Enabling DAI without DHCP snooping bindings, or forgetting to trust the uplink ports.
lessons.scenario: A school complains that students occasionally get a wrong gateway address from the Wi-Fi VLAN. Investigation finds a student-owned router with DHCP enabled plugged into a classroom wall port. The engineer enables ip dhcp snooping on the VLAN and marks only the uplink as trusted, so the rogue server's offers are dropped. They then enable DAI on the same VLAN with the uplink trusted, add port security with maximum 2 to prevent small switches on access ports, and write an extended ACL denying student subnets from reaching the staff subnet, applied inbound near the students, with a final permit ip any any.
lessons.onTheJob: Edit ACLs through a console or out-of-band session, and test them on a lab or with a scheduled reload, because a bad ACL on the interface that carries your SSH session locks you out. Use named ACLs and sequence numbers so you can insert lines without deleting the whole list, add remarks to explain intent, and use the log keyword sparingly because it burns CPU. On switches, roll out DHCP snooping before DAI and watch for legitimate devices with static addresses, which need static bindings or DAI will drop their ARPs. Set sensible port-security maximums for places with IP phones and PCs, and use error-disable recovery so a noisy port does not need a manual reset.

cheatSheet.heading: Models, PDUs, TCP vs UDP and ports
points: OSI: 1 Physical, 2 Data Link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application. TCP/IP: Link, Internet, Transport, Application.
Encapsulation down the stack: data, segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP), packet, frame, bits. Switches forward frames; routers forward packets.
Across a router the frame header is rewritten at every hop; IP source and destination stay end to end (unless NAT is used).
TCP: three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), sequencing, acknowledgements, retransmission, windowing. UDP: connectionless, low overhead, no recovery.
Ports to know: FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, DHCP 67/68 (UDP), TFTP 69 (UDP), HTTP 80, NTP 123 (UDP), SNMP 161/162 (UDP), HTTPS 443, syslog 514 (UDP).

cheatSheet.heading: Devices, topologies, cabling and interface errors
points: Layer 2 switch: frames by MAC, per-VLAN broadcast domain. Router and layer 3 switch: packets by IP. NGFW: application-aware. IPS: inline blocking. WLC: manages lightweight APs.
Topologies: two-tier (collapsed core) for small campuses, three-tier (access, distribution, core) for large ones, spine-leaf for data centres with east-west traffic.
Copper UTP maximum 100 m per segment. Single-mode fiber: laser, kilometres. Multimode: cheaper optics, shorter distance.
PoE: 802.3af about 15.4 W, 802.3at about 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60 W or 90 W per port. A device that will not boot may have too low a PoE class or budget.
CRC errors and runts point to bad cables or duplex mismatch; late collisions point to half-duplex or duplex mismatch; a mismatch leaves the link up but slow.
Switching: learn from the source MAC, forward by the destination MAC, flood unknown unicast and broadcast out all other ports in the VLAN. MAC aging default 300 s.

cheatSheet.heading: IPv4 subnetting quick reference
points: Usable hosts = 2^h - 2. Block sizes in the interesting octet: /25 128, /26 64, /27 32, /28 16, /29 8, /30 4. Usable hosts: 126, 62, 30, 14, 6, 2.
Network address = first address of the block, broadcast = last. Example 172.16.45.200/20: block 16 in octet 3, network 172.16.32.0, broadcast 172.16.47.255.
VLSM: sort by size, allocate largest first, never overlap, use /30 for point-to-point links.

cheatSheet.heading: IPv6, wireless and virtualization essentials
points: IPv6 is 128 bits in eight hex groups; drop leading zeros, one :: only. LANs are /64. Global unicast 2000::/3, unique local FC00::/7 (FD), link-local FE80::/10, multicast FF00::/8.
FF02::1 all nodes, FF02::2 all routers, solicited-node FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx replaces ARP. IPv6 has no broadcast. Anycast: same address on several devices, nearest answers.
Modified EUI-64: split the MAC, insert FFFE, flip the seventh bit. SLAAC builds an address from the router-advertised prefix.
2.4 GHz non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11. 5 GHz has many more. SSID is the name, BSSID the AP radio MAC. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, WPA3 adds SAE; WEP and TKIP are obsolete.
Type 1 hypervisor runs on bare metal, Type 2 on a host OS. Containers share the host kernel. VRF gives one router multiple routing tables.

cheatSheet.heading: VLANs, trunks, STP, EtherChannel and discovery
points: VLAN = broadcast domain = subnet. Access port: one VLAN, untagged. Trunk: many VLANs with 802.1Q 4-byte tag; native VLAN untagged and must match. Normal range 1-1005.
Inter-VLAN routing: router-on-a-stick (subinterfaces with encapsulation dot1q), SVIs plus ip routing on a layer 3 switch, routed port with no switchport. Use allowed vlan add to extend a trunk.
STP: lowest bridge ID (priority + MAC) is root. Costs 10M 100, 100M 19, 1G 4, 10G 2. Timers 2/15/20 s, classic convergence up to about 50 s. Every port on the root is designated.
RSTP: discarding, learning, forwarding; adds alternate and backup roles. Rapid PVST+: spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst. PortFast and BPDU Guard on access ports only.
EtherChannel: LACP active/passive, PAgP desirable/auto, on forces; at least one side must initiate and protocols cannot be mixed. Members must match. Verify with show etherchannel summary (SU, P).
CDP: Cisco, on by default, 60 s hello, 180 s holdtime. LLDP: IEEE 802.1AB, off by default (lldp run), 30 s and 120 s. Verify with show cdp neighbors and show lldp neighbors.

cheatSheet.heading: Wireless architectures, management access and automation
points: Architectures: autonomous APs, controller-based (lightweight APs, CAPWAP on UDP 5246 and 5247, WLC), cloud-based (Meraki). AP modes: local, FlexConnect, monitor, sniffer, rogue detector, bridge, SE-Connect.
Local-mode AP: access port, traffic tunnelled to the WLC. FlexConnect AP: trunk, locally switched WLANs, survives WAN loss. WLC LAG pairs with a static EtherChannel (on). Service port is out-of-band.

Management: console (local), SSH 22 and HTTPS 443 (encrypted), Telnet 23 and HTTP 80 (clear text). TACACS+ (TCP 49, full encryption, per-command authorization) vs RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813, password only).

SDN: controller holds the control plane; devices keep the data plane. Northbound API to applications (REST), southbound to devices (NETCONF, CLI, OpenFlow). Underlay = IP transport, overlay = tunnels (VXLAN), fabric = both.
REST: POST create, GET read, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE delete. Status: 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500. JSON: braces, brackets, double-quoted keys. YAML: indentation. XML: tags.

Ansible: agentless, push, YAML playbooks. Puppet and Chef: agent-based, pull. Terraform: declarative infrastructure as code with plan and apply. Predictive AI forecasts; generative AI drafts and must be reviewed.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: The CCNA 200-301 exam is 120 minutes, delivered through Pearson VUE (in a test centre or online). Cisco does not publish the number of questions; it is commonly reported at around 100 to 120, so plan for about one minute per question.
Cisco reports scores on a 300-1000 scale and does not publish the passing score; it is widely reported near 825 and can vary by form, so aim for comfortable mastery rather than the minimum.

Expect multiple choice (single and multiple answer), drag-and-drop, and simulation or testlet questions where you read device output or configure devices. Cisco exams generally do not allow returning to an earlier question, so answer each one carefully before moving on.
Subnetting should be automatic before the exam: block sizes, masks and wildcards from memory. Work numeric questions on the provided note board and double-check the interesting octet.
Read the exact wording: "choose two" means two answers, "BEST" means more than one option works, and output questions often hinge on one line such as a state, flag or counter.
For simulations, verify your work with show commands and do not break existing configuration; use the question text as the authoritative list of requirements.

cheatSheet.heading: What changes in CCNA v2.0 (from February 3, 2027)
points: Same exam code (200-301) and 120-minute format, but a new version of the exam topics. Sources agree the first v2.0 test date is February 3, 2027, with v1.1 exams available through February 2, 2027. Confirm dates on the Cisco Learning Network, which publishes both outlines.

This study track targets v1.1 (six domains: Network Fundamentals 20%, Network Access 20%, IP Connectivity 25%, IP Services 10%, Security Fundamentals 15%, Automation and Programmability 10%), which is the current version until v2.0 starts.

v2.0 is reported to consolidate those into five domains: Network Infrastructure and Connectivity 25%, Switching and Network Access 25%, IP Routing 20%, Network Services and Security 20%, and AI, Network Operations and Management 10%.

New in v2.0 is a dedicated AI domain covering AI in network operations, including evaluating output from agentic AI and digital network assistants. The v1.1 AI and machine learning topic you study here (predictive vs generative AI, ML) is the foundation for it.

v2.0 is reported to put more weight on troubleshooting and diagnose-style tasks, for example wired and wireless client connectivity, DHCP and DNS troubleshooting and PoE. The v1.1 material on interface errors, duplex, VLAN and trunk faults, STP and EtherChannel verification applies directly.

Third-party summaries report that the standalone Automation and Programmability domain is retired in v2.0, with Ansible and monitoring topics (SNMP, syslog) combined into the operations domain and REST, JSON and Terraform no longer listed. Treat that as unconfirmed until you read Cisco's v2.0 topics; for any exam taken before February 3, 2027, v1.1 including REST, JSON and SDN is what counts.

Fundamentals, VLANs, trunking, STP, EtherChannel, wireless architectures and IP addressing remain core in both versions, so this track's Network Fundamentals and Network Access content carries over to v2.0 with little change.

cheatSheet.heading: Route selection and administrative distance
points: Order of decision: (1) longest prefix match, (2) lowest administrative distance for the identical prefix, (3) lowest metric within one protocol; equal-cost paths are load-shared.
AD values: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, internal EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, external EIGRP 170, iBGP 200, 255 = unusable.

Routing table line: O 10.2.0.0/16 [110/20] via 192.168.1.2 means OSPF route, AD 110, metric 20. Codes: C connected, L local /32, S static, S* candidate default, O OSPF, O IA inter-area, O E1/E2 external, D EIGRP, R RIP, B BGP.

Static: ip route network mask next-hop [AD]; default ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 next-hop; IPv6 needs ipv6 unicast-routing and ipv6 route ::/0 next-hop. A link-local next hop needs the exit interface too.
Floating static route: AD higher than the primary (for example 150 behind OSPF at 110) so it appears only when the primary route disappears.
No match and no default means drop plus ICMP unreachable (U on a ping). A static route with an unresolvable next hop is not installed.

cheatSheet.heading: OSPFv2 single-area and first-hop redundancy
points: Link-state, IP protocol 89, multicast 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR). Area 0 is the backbone; the process ID is locally significant.
Neighbor must-match list: area ID, subnet and mask, Hello/Dead timers (10/40 on Ethernet and point-to-point), authentication, stub flag; router IDs unique; MTU mismatch stalls ExStart/Exchange.
States: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full. 2WAY/DROTHER between two non-DR routers is normal.
DR/BDR: highest priority (0-255, default 1), then highest router ID; priority 0 never; election is non-preemptive. Point-to-point network type has no election.
Router ID order: router-id command, highest up loopback, highest up physical interface. It changes only when the process restarts (clear ip ospf process).

Cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth, minimum 1, default reference 100 Mbps: Fast Ethernet and faster = 1, 10 Mbps = 10, T1 = 64. Path metric = sum of outgoing interface costs. auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 makes Gigabit = 10.
Config: router ospf 1, router-id x, network address wildcard area 0 (or ip ospf 1 area 0 on the interface), passive-interface for edge links, default-information originate for a default route.
Verify: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface brief, show ip protocols, show ip route ospf.

FHRP: routers share a virtual IP and MAC and hosts use the virtual IP as gateway. HSRP: Cisco-proprietary, active/standby, priority 100, preempt OFF by default (show standby brief). VRRP: open standard, master/backup, preempt ON by default. GLBP: Cisco-proprietary, one group load-balances using several virtual MACs.
HSRP and VRRP leave the standby router idle per group; use two groups with opposite priorities per VLAN, or GLBP, to use both. Tracking lowers priority when an uplink fails.

cheatSheet.heading: NAT, DHCP, DNS and NTP facts
points: NAT terms: inside local = private host address, inside global = translated address seen outside; outside local/global describe the remote host. Static = permanent one-to-one; dynamic = pool; PAT/overload = many-to-one using ports.

NAT config: ip nat inside / ip nat outside on interfaces; ACL selects hosts to translate (it does not filter); ip nat inside source list N interface X overload. Verify: show ip nat translations and statistics, clear ip nat translation *.

DHCP: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA); UDP 67 server and 68 client; relay with ip helper-address on the CLIENT-facing interface; ip dhcp excluded-address and ip dhcp pool; 169.254.x.x = no DHCP answer.
DNS: UDP/TCP 53; A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias, MX = mail, NS = name server, PTR = reverse. Ping by IP works but ping by name fails = DNS problem.
NTP: UDP 123; stratum 1 attached to a reference clock, +1 per hop, 16 = unsynchronized; ntp server address; show ntp status, show ntp associations.

cheatSheet.heading: SNMP, syslog, QoS, SSH and file transfer
points: SNMP: manager polls agent on UDP 161, traps and informs go to UDP 162; informs are acknowledged. v1 and v2c use clear-text community strings; v3 authPriv = authentication plus encryption.
Syslog: UDP 514; severities 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging; a threshold includes every more severe (lower) level; logging host x.

QoS: classify, mark (CoS 3 bits in 802.1Q, DSCP 6 bits in IP), queue (FIFO, CBWFQ, LLQ priority queue), avoid congestion (WRED). Voice = EF (46), needs about 150 ms delay, 30 ms jitter, 1 percent loss or less.
Policing drops or remarks excess traffic with no buffer; shaping buffers and delays excess traffic to smooth it.
SSH TCP 22 (encrypted) vs Telnet TCP 23 (clear). SSH needs hostname, domain name, crypto key generate rsa, local user, login local and transport input ssh on vty.
TFTP UDP 69, no authentication, lab use; FTP TCP 21 plus data, has credentials but no encryption; SCP/SFTP use SSH.

cheatSheet.heading: Security concepts, AAA and VPNs
points: Threat = what could cause harm, vulnerability = weakness, exploit = method that abuses it, risk = likelihood times impact, mitigation = control. CIA = confidentiality, integrity, availability.

Attacks: DoS/DDoS, spoofing, reflection/amplification, man-in-the-middle, reconnaissance, malware (virus needs a host, worm self-spreads, trojan disguises, ransomware encrypts), phishing, spear phishing, vishing, brute-force and dictionary password attacks.
Security program: user awareness, user training, physical access control. MFA = two or more different factor types (know, have, are).
Device access: enable secret (strong hash, overrides enable password), line or local logins, exec-timeout, login block-for; service password-encryption = weak reversible type 7.

AAA: authentication (who), authorization (what), accounting (what did you do). RADIUS = open, UDP 1812/1813, combines authentication and authorization, encrypts only the password. TACACS+ = TCP 49, separates AAA, encrypts the whole payload, per-command authorization. 802.1X = port-based access control.

VPNs: site-to-site (gateway to gateway, usually IPsec, hosts unaware); remote-access (user to gateway, client software or SSL/TLS). IPsec = confidentiality, integrity, authentication (ESP/AH, IKE); GRE = tunnel only, no encryption.

cheatSheet.heading: ACLs, Layer 2 security and wireless security
points: Standard ACL 1-99 and 1300-1999 matches source only, place near the destination. Extended 100-199 and 2000-2699 matches protocol, source, destination, ports; place near the source. Top-down first match; implicit deny any at the end.

Apply with ip access-group in|out (one per protocol, per direction, per interface); vty protection with access-class; outbound ACLs do not filter router-generated traffic; check with show access-lists.
Port security: default max 1 MAC, violation default shutdown (err-disabled), restrict logs and drops, protect drops silently; sticky learns and saves addresses.
DHCP snooping: untrusted ports drop DHCP server messages, builds the binding table. DAI validates ARP against that table; trust uplinks and enable snooping first.

Wireless: WEP broken; WPA = TKIP; WPA2 = AES-CCMP, Personal PSK (8-63 ASCII) or Enterprise 802.1X with RADIUS; WPA3 = SAE, protected management frames mandatory. Hiding the SSID and MAC filtering are not real security.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode on a switch, display a brief list of the VLANs and the access ports assigned to each.
cliChallenges.explanation: show vlan brief lists each VLAN, its name, status and the access ports in it. Trunk ports do not appear in the list, so use show interfaces trunk for those.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode on a switch, create VLAN 20 and enter VLAN configuration mode.
cliChallenges.explanation: vlan 20 creates the VLAN in the VLAN database (vlan.dat) if it does not already exist. Normal-range VLANs are 1 to 1005.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a switch port that connects to a PC, force the port to be a static access port.
cliChallenges.explanation: switchport mode access disables trunk negotiation on the port so it carries a single VLAN untagged. It is the standard hardening step for edge ports.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on an access port, assign the port to VLAN 20.
cliChallenges.explanation: switchport access vlan sets the data VLAN of an access port. The VLAN must exist, otherwise the port ends up in an inactive state on many platforms.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on an inter-switch port, set the port to trunk unconditionally.
cliChallenges.explanation: switchport mode trunk hard-codes the port as a trunk. Pair it with switchport nonegotiate (or an explicit mode on both ends) so DTP does not decide the link type.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a trunk port, restrict the trunk so it carries only VLANs 10 and 20.
cliChallenges.explanation: switchport trunk allowed vlan sets the allowed list, replacing any previous list. Use the add keyword to append a VLAN to an existing list instead.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display the interfaces that are operating as trunks together with their native VLAN and allowed VLANs.
cliChallenges.explanation: show interfaces trunk reports mode, encapsulation, status, native VLAN, allowed VLANs and the VLANs currently forwarding and not pruned.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, enable the Cisco per-VLAN rapid spanning tree mode.
cliChallenges.explanation: spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst runs a separate RSTP instance per VLAN for convergence in seconds instead of the 30 to 50 seconds of classic STP.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, make this switch the root bridge for VLAN 10 by lowering its priority automatically with the root macro.
cliChallenges.explanation: The root primary macro sets the priority low enough (usually 24576, or lower than the current root) to win the election. Use root secondary on the backup switch.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on an access port that connects to an end host, make the port skip the listening and learning states.
cliChallenges.explanation: PortFast moves the port directly to forwarding. Use it only on host-facing ports and combine it with BPDU Guard.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a physical member port, add it to EtherChannel 1 using LACP and actively initiate negotiation.
cliChallenges.explanation: channel-group 1 mode active uses LACP active mode to bundle the port into Port-channel 1. The other end must be active or passive, and the member settings must match.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display a one-line-per-channel summary of the EtherChannels and their member port flags.
cliChallenges.explanation: The summary shows each Port-channel, its protocol and the flags for members. SU on the Port-channel and P on the members means a healthy layer 2 bundle.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, enable LLDP on the switch.
cliChallenges.explanation: LLDP is disabled by default on Cisco IOS devices and lldp run enables it globally; CDP, by contrast, is on by default.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display detailed CDP information, including neighbor management IP addresses.
cliChallenges.explanation: The detail form adds each neighbor's IP address, software version and native VLAN, which the plain neighbors list omits.

cliChallenges.prompt: In subinterface configuration mode on a router (interface g0/0.20), tag the subinterface for VLAN 20 using IEEE 802.1Q.
cliChallenges.explanation: encapsulation dot1q 20 tells the subinterface to send and receive frames tagged with VLAN 20, which is the heart of router-on-a-stick. The IP address is configured after it.

cliChallenges.prompt: In VTY line configuration mode, allow only SSH for incoming remote management sessions.
cliChallenges.explanation: transport input ssh blocks Telnet on the lines and permits only encrypted SSH sessions.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a router, assign the IPv4 address 192.168.10.1 with a /24 mask.
cliChallenges.explanation: IOS takes the mask in dotted-decimal form, not as a prefix length. 255.255.255.0 is /24.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a router, assign the IPv6 global unicast address 2001:db8:1:1::1 with a /64 prefix.
cliChallenges.explanation: ipv6 address takes the address and prefix length in slash notation. IPv6 interfaces also need ipv6 unicast-routing globally if the router is to forward IPv6 packets.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a router, set the IPv6 link-local address to FE80::1.
cliChallenges.explanation: Adding the link-local keyword makes IOS treat the address as a link-local address and replaces the automatically generated one, which makes neighbor next hops easy to remember.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display a one-line summary of the IPv4 address and status of every interface.
cliChallenges.explanation: show ip interface brief is the fastest overview: address, status (administrative) and protocol (line) for each interface, including SVIs.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode on a router, create a static route to the 10.1.0.0/16 network through the next-hop address 192.168.1.2.
cliChallenges.explanation: A static route is ip route network subnet-mask next-hop. It uses a normal subnet mask (255.255.0.0 for a /16), not a wildcard mask, and gets administrative distance 1 by default.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode on a branch router, configure a default route that sends all unknown traffic to the ISP router at 203.0.113.1.
cliChallenges.explanation: A default route uses destination 0.0.0.0 and mask 0.0.0.0, which matches everything but, as the shortest possible prefix, is used only when no more specific route exists.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, create a floating static default route via 198.51.100.1 that stays hidden behind an OSPF default route (AD 110) until OSPF fails. Use administrative distance 150.
cliChallenges.explanation: The trailing number is the administrative distance. Because 150 is higher than OSPF's 110, the static route is not installed until the OSPF default route is withdrawn.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, create an IPv6 default route with next hop 2001:db8:1::1.
cliChallenges.explanation: The IPv6 default prefix is ::/0. The router also needs ipv6 unicast-routing enabled to forward IPv6 packets.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode on a router, enter OSPFv2 router configuration mode using process ID 1.
cliChallenges.explanation: router ospf process-id starts the OSPF process. The process ID is only locally significant, so it does not need to match on neighboring routers.

cliChallenges.prompt: In OSPF router configuration mode (config-router), manually set the router ID to 1.1.1.1.
cliChallenges.explanation: A manual router ID overrides the loopback and physical-interface selection. It takes effect when the OSPF process restarts, for example with clear ip ospf process.

cliChallenges.prompt: In OSPF router configuration mode, enable OSPF in area 0 on every interface whose address is inside 10.1.1.0/24.
cliChallenges.explanation: The network command takes a wildcard mask (0.0.0.255 for a /24) and the area number. Interfaces whose addresses fall in that range join OSPF and their subnet is advertised.

cliChallenges.prompt: In OSPF router configuration mode, stop OSPF from sending Hellos out the user-facing interface GigabitEthernet0/2 while still advertising its subnet.
cliChallenges.explanation: A passive interface sends no Hellos and forms no adjacencies, but its connected network is still advertised. This is best practice on edge interfaces facing users.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display the OSPF neighbors with their state, role and interface.
cliChallenges.explanation: show ip ospf neighbor lists router ID, priority, state/role (such as FULL/DR), dead time, address and interface. It is the first check when OSPF routes are missing.

cliChallenges.prompt: In privileged EXEC mode, display only the routes in the routing table that were learned through OSPF.
cliChallenges.explanation: Adding a protocol keyword filters the routing table. OSPF routes are shown with the code O and the [110/cost] pair.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode, make this router ineligible to become the OSPF DR or BDR on this segment.
cliChallenges.explanation: An OSPF interface priority of 0 removes the router from the DR and BDR election. The default priority is 1 and the highest value wins.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on a router's LAN interface, join HSRP group 10 with the virtual IP address 10.10.10.1.
cliChallenges.explanation: standby group ip virtual-address configures HSRP. Hosts then use the virtual IP as their default gateway; add standby 10 priority and standby 10 preempt to control which router is active.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on the LAN-facing router interface, mark it as a NAT inside interface.
cliChallenges.explanation: NAT needs each participating interface labeled: ip nat inside on the private side and ip nat outside on the Internet-facing side.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, translate the hosts matched by access list 1 using the address of GigabitEthernet0/0, with many-to-one port translation.
cliChallenges.command: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload
altCommands: ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/0 overload
cliChallenges.explanation: This is PAT: the ACL selects which inside hosts are translated, interface names the outside address to share, and overload lets many hosts share it using unique port numbers.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, publish the internal server 10.0.5.20 at the public address 203.0.113.20 with a permanent one-to-one translation.
cliChallenges.explanation: Static NAT maps one inside local address to one inside global address permanently, so outside clients can initiate connections to the server.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on the client-facing interface, relay DHCP broadcasts to the DHCP server at 10.0.100.5.
cliChallenges.explanation: ip helper-address turns the client's DHCP broadcast into a unicast to the server and lets the server choose the correct pool. It belongs on the interface that receives the clients' broadcasts.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, prevent the addresses 10.0.0.1 through 10.0.0.10 from being handed out by the router's DHCP server.
cliChallenges.explanation: Excluded addresses are removed from the pools so gateways, servers and printers with static addresses never collide with leases.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, configure the router as an NTP client of the server 10.1.1.1.
cliChallenges.explanation: ntp server address synchronizes the clock to an upstream source. Verify with show ntp status and show ntp associations.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, send the router's log messages to the syslog server at 10.9.9.9.
cliChallenges.explanation: logging host sets the syslog destination (UDP 514 by default). The logging trap command sets the severity threshold and service timestamps adds times to the messages.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, set the privileged EXEC password to the hashed secret C1sc0Secret.
cliChallenges.explanation: enable secret stores the password as a one-way salted hash and takes precedence over enable password, which would be kept as plain text or reversible type 7.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, obscure all plain-text passwords in the configuration with the reversible type 7 scheme.
cliChallenges.explanation: service password-encryption stops passwords from being readable at a glance in the configuration, but type 7 is trivially reversible; it is not a replacement for enable secret.

cliChallenges.prompt: In line configuration mode for the vty lines, allow only SSH for incoming remote management sessions.
cliChallenges.explanation: transport input ssh refuses Telnet and other protocols on the vty lines. It must be combined with an RSA key, a domain name and login local with a local user.

cliChallenges.prompt: In global configuration mode, add an entry to extended ACL 101 that denies Telnet (TCP port 23) from the 10.1.1.0/24 network to the host 192.168.5.10.
altCommands: access-list 101 deny tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.5.10 eq telnet
cliChallenges.explanation: Extended ACL syntax is protocol, source and wildcard, destination, then the port operator. Telnet is TCP port 23, and a permit ip any any is usually needed after the deny so other traffic still passes.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode, apply access list 101 to filter traffic entering this interface.
cliChallenges.explanation: ip access-group number-or-name in|out binds the ACL to an interface and direction. Extended ACLs are normally applied inbound close to the source of the traffic.

cliChallenges.prompt: In interface configuration mode on an access port, limit the port to two learned MAC addresses with port security.
cliChallenges.explanation: The port-security maximum command sets how many MAC addresses are allowed. Port security must also be enabled with switchport port-security, and the default violation mode is shutdown.

madlibs.scenario: A subnet using the prefix /26 has the mask {b1} and offers {b2} usable host addresses, because two of the 64 addresses are reserved for the network address and the {b3} address.
madlibs.explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses and 62 usable. The mask in the last octet is 192 (11000000). The reserved pair is the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address.

madlibs.scenario: A switch builds its MAC address table by reading the {b1} MAC address of each incoming frame. It chooses the egress port by looking up the {b2} MAC address, and when that address is not in the table it {b3} the frame out every other port in the VLAN.
madlibs.explanation: Switches learn from sources and forward by destinations. An unknown unicast is flooded out all ports except the arrival port, and the reply then teaches the switch the missing entry.

madlibs.scenario: The switch with the lowest {b1} wins the spanning-tree election and becomes the root bridge. {b2} is enabled on access ports facing end hosts so they forward immediately, and {b3} err-disables such a port if a BPDU ever arrives.
madlibs.explanation: The bridge ID is priority plus MAC, and the lowest wins. PortFast skips listening and learning on edge ports, and BPDU Guard protects that shortcut by shutting the port when a switch appears.

madlibs.scenario: An 802.1Q trunk inserts a {b1}-byte tag into each frame that carries a 12-bit VLAN ID. Frames in the {b2} VLAN cross the trunk without a tag, and a router-on-a-stick uses one {b3} per VLAN on a single physical interface.
madlibs.explanation: The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes. The native VLAN is the untagged one and must match on both ends. A router-on-a-stick uses subinterfaces, each with encapsulation dot1q and its own IP address; SVIs belong to layer 3 switches.

madlibs.scenario: In a REST API, creating a resource uses the HTTP verb {b1}, reading it uses {b2}, and removing it uses {b3}. The interface that lets an application talk to an SDN controller is called the {b4} API.
madlibs.explanation: CRUD maps to POST, GET, PUT or PATCH, and DELETE. Applications use the northbound API of the controller, while the controller uses southbound protocols to reach the devices.

madlibs.scenario: Four routers share one Ethernet segment. R1 has priority 100 and router ID 1.1.1.1; R2 has priority 1 and router ID 9.9.9.9. The DR will be {b1}, because {b2} is compared before the router ID. A router configured with priority {b3} can never become DR or BDR.
madlibs.explanation: The highest OSPF priority wins first and the router ID is only the tie-breaker, so R1 beats R2 despite its lower router ID. Priority 0 removes a router from the DR and BDR election entirely.

madlibs.scenario: A router holds 10.0.0.0/8 learned from OSPF and 10.1.1.0/24 learned from RIP. A packet for 10.1.1.5 follows the {b1} route because of longest prefix match. If the identical prefix 10.1.1.0/24 were offered by both OSPF and RIP, the {b2} route would be installed because it has the lower {b3}.
madlibs.explanation: The /24 is more specific than the /8 so it wins first, regardless of the protocol. Only for identical prefixes does administrative distance decide, and OSPF (110) is preferred to RIP (120).

madlibs.scenario: A host's private address is its inside {b1} address, while the address the Internet sees after translation is its inside {b2} address. When hundreds of hosts share a single public address by using unique source ports, the feature is called {b3}.
madlibs.explanation: Inside local is the real private address and inside global is the translated, publicly visible one. PAT distinguishes many flows on one public address by port number; static NAT maps one-to-one and dynamic NAT draws from a pool.

madlibs.scenario: An ACL is processed from the {b1}, and the first matching entry decides. Traffic that matches no entry is dropped by the implicit {b2} at the end. A standard ACL, which matches only the source address, is normally placed close to the {b3}.
madlibs.explanation: ACLs are read top to bottom with first-match logic and finish with an invisible deny any. A standard ACL cannot specify a destination, so placing it near the destination avoids blocking the source from everything else.

madlibs.scenario: In DHCP, the client broadcasts a Discover, the server replies with an {b1}, the client broadcasts a Request and the server finishes with an {b2}. When the server sits on another subnet, the client-facing router interface needs {b3} so the broadcast is relayed as a unicast.
madlibs.explanation: The exchange is Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. ip helper-address on the interface facing the clients relays the broadcast to the server and lets it pick the right pool.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for a client obtaining an IPv4 address from a DHCP server (DORA).
steps: The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER to find servers
A server answers with a DHCPOFFER containing an address and options
The client broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST for the offered address
The server confirms with a DHCPACK and the client starts using the address
sequences.explanation: DORA stands for Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The request is also broadcast so that any other servers whose offers were not chosen know to withdraw them.

sequences.prompt: Put these spanning-tree decisions in the order in which the protocol makes them.
steps: Switches exchange BPDUs and elect the root bridge with the lowest bridge ID
Each non-root switch selects its root port, the port with the lowest root path cost
On each segment, one designated port is chosen toward the root
All remaining ports are placed in the blocking (alternate) role
sequences.explanation: The root bridge must exist first because every cost is measured toward it. Root ports and designated ports are then elected, and any port that is neither is blocked to break the loop.

sequences.prompt: Order the PDUs a sender creates as a web page request moves down the TCP/IP stack.
steps: Application data is generated by the web browser
TCP adds port numbers and sequence numbers, creating a segment
IP adds source and destination addresses, creating a packet
Ethernet adds MAC addresses and a trailer, creating a frame
The frame is transmitted as bits on the medium
sequences.explanation: Encapsulation proceeds from the top layer down: data, segment, packet, frame, bits. The receiver decapsulates in the reverse order, stripping one header at each layer.

sequences.prompt: Order the events when a switch with an empty MAC address table receives the first frame from host A to host B.
steps: The frame arrives on the port to which host A is connected
The switch records host A's source MAC address against that port in the MAC address table
The switch looks up the destination MAC address and finds no entry
The switch floods the frame out all other ports in the VLAN
Host B replies and the switch learns B's MAC address, so later frames are forwarded out one port only
sequences.explanation: Learning happens on the source address as the frame arrives, then the destination lookup decides forwarding or flooding. The reply from B teaches the switch the missing entry so the exchange is no longer flooded.

sequences.prompt: Put the OSPF neighbor states in the order two routers pass through them on the way to a fully synchronized adjacency.
steps: Down: no Hello has been received from the neighbor
Init: a Hello was received but our router ID is not yet listed in it
2-Way: our router ID appears in the neighbor Hello, so communication is bidirectional and the DR and BDR are elected
ExStart: the two routers agree who is master and set the starting sequence number for database exchange
Exchange: database description packets summarize the LSAs each router holds
Loading: link-state requests and updates fetch the LSAs that are missing or newer
Full: the link-state databases are synchronized and the adjacency is complete
sequences.explanation: Hellos establish bidirectional communication (Init to 2-Way). After the DR and BDR are chosen, the routers negotiate roles (ExStart), summarize their databases (Exchange), request what they lack (Loading) and finish at Full. MTU mismatches commonly stall at ExStart or Exchange.

sequences.prompt: A client in VLAN 20 gets an address from a DHCP server on another subnet through a relay. Put the steps in order.
steps: The client broadcasts a DHCP Discover on its VLAN
The router interface with ip helper-address converts it to a unicast, adding its own address in the giaddr field, and sends it to the server
The server selects the pool that matches giaddr and replies with an Offer through the relay
The relay delivers the Offer to the client, which broadcasts a Request for the offered address
The relay forwards the Request as a unicast to the server
The server sends an Acknowledge, and the client begins using the leased address and options
sequences.explanation: The client cannot know the server's address, so its first message is a broadcast. The relay unicasts to the server and stamps giaddr so the server can choose the matching pool; the Request and Acknowledge follow the same relayed path.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for an inside host reaching an Internet server through a PAT router.
steps: The inside host sends a packet with source 192.168.1.10:51000 toward the server
The router receives it on an ip nat inside interface and routes it toward the outside interface
The router matches the source against the NAT ACL, creates an entry and rewrites the source to 203.0.113.5:1024
The packet is forwarded to the Internet server, which replies to 203.0.113.5:1024
The router finds the entry for that inside global address and port and rewrites the destination back to 192.168.1.10:51000
The reply is forwarded to the inside host
sequences.explanation: Translation is created when an inside host sends outbound traffic that matches the NAT ACL. The table entry, which pairs the inside local and inside global address and port, is what lets the router reverse the translation for the reply.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps in order for introducing a new extended ACL to a production router safely.
steps: Write down which traffic must be denied or permitted, and in which direction on which interface
Create the named extended ACL with the specific entries first and a final permit ip any any if only some traffic is to be blocked
Review the ACL with show access-lists and check the wildcard masks
Apply it with ip access-group in or out on the chosen interface, keeping an out-of-band path in case of a lockout
Test traffic that should be allowed and traffic that should be denied, and watch the match counters
sequences.explanation: Plan first, because an ACL is order-sensitive and ends in an implicit deny. Build and review it before applying it, then test both directions of intent and confirm the counters increment on the expected entries.

caseStudies.title: Harbor Dental Group's New Clinic Floor
caseStudies.scenario: Harbor Dental Group opens a second-floor clinic with an access switch (SW-B) that connects to the main floor's switch (SW-A) over a single trunk. Staff PCs are in VLAN 10 and Cisco IP phones are in voice VLAN 20. Each PC plugs into a phone and the phone plugs into the wall port. A router at the main office provides inter-VLAN routing using a single trunk to SW-A. After the cutover, PCs on both floors work, but the new-floor phones cannot register with the call manager on the main floor. Engineers find that show interfaces trunk on SW-A lists allowed VLANs 1,10 only, and that the router's subinterface for VLAN 20 exists but shows no encapsulation line. A log message on SW-B also reports a native VLAN mismatch, because SW-A uses VLAN 99 as native and SW-B was left at the default. Finally, the owner asks for the floor ports to be hardened so that a patient cannot plug a personal switch into a wall jack and cause a loop. The team is also planning a second uplink between the two switches for resilience.

questions.question: Which command, run on SW-A, best confirms why voice VLAN traffic does not cross the trunk?
questions.explanation: show interfaces trunk displays the allowed VLAN list and the VLANs actually forwarding, which shows VLAN 20 missing. CDP lists neighbors, ip route is layer 3 and the STP summary covers loop prevention, not VLAN permission.

questions.question: How should VLAN 20 be added to the trunk without disturbing the VLANs already allowed?
questions.explanation: The add keyword appends VLAN 20 to the existing list. Without it the command would replace the list, dropping VLANs 1 and 10. Access mode and the voice VLAN command are access-port settings.

questions.question: Which two actions complete the fix for the router and the trunk? (Choose two.)
options: Set the native VLAN on SW-B's trunk to 99 to match SW-A
Configure encapsulation dot1q 20 on the VLAN 20 subinterface
Enable PortFast on the trunk between the switches
Change the router subinterface to an SVI
questions.explanation: A subinterface needs encapsulation dot1q with its VLAN ID before it can process tagged frames, and the native VLAN must match on both ends of the trunk. PortFast does not belong on trunks, and an SVI is a layer 3 switch construct rather than a router subinterface.

questions.question: Which pair of features best protects the wall-jack access ports against a patient plugging in a personal switch?
questions.explanation: PortFast gives hosts quick access and BPDU Guard err-disables the port as soon as a BPDU from a switch arrives. Dynamic trunking, native VLAN 1 and bundling protocols would make the ports less safe or are unrelated.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Logistics' Addressing Plan
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Logistics is opening a regional depot and has been given 192.168.50.0/24 for the site. The depot needs four IPv4 segments: an office LAN for 60 hosts, a warehouse scanner LAN for 25 hosts, a management LAN for 10 devices, and a router-to-router link to the main office. The network engineer plans to use VLSM, allocating the largest subnet first and moving upward without leaving gaps. The depot router will also receive a global unicast IPv6 /48 prefix, and the engineer will assign a /64 to each LAN and let clients configure themselves using SLAAC. The routing team plans to advertise the networks with OSPF network statements, so the engineer also needs the wildcard masks. Finally, the engineer remembers that each router interface automatically has an IPv6 address starting with FE80 that the routing protocol will use to reach neighbours on the link, and wonders whether that address can be used for the next hop of a static route.

questions.question: Which prefix length should the 60-host office LAN use to waste the least space?
questions.explanation: 60 hosts need 6 host bits (2^6 - 2 = 62 usable), so /26. A /27 provides only 30 usable hosts, /28 only 14, and /25 provides 126 and wastes space.

questions.question: The office LAN takes 192.168.50.0/26 and the scanner LAN takes the next /27. Which network address should the 10-device management LAN, using a /28, start at?
questions.explanation: The /26 occupies .0 to .63 and the next /27 occupies .64 to .95, so the next free address is 192.168.50.96, where a /28 (.96 to .111) fits with 14 usable hosts. .64 is already used and the others would leave unnecessary gaps or overlap.

questions.question: What wildcard mask would the OSPF network statement use for the /28 management LAN?
questions.explanation: The /28 mask is 255.255.255.240, and 255 minus 240 is 15, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.15. 0.0.0.16 is the block size, 0.0.0.240 is the mask's own octet and 0.0.0.7 would match a /29.

questions.question: An IPv6 link-local address can serve as a next-hop address for a route to a neighbor on the same link, as long as the outgoing interface is also specified.
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses are valid on the attached link, and routing protocols and static routes use them as next hops, but because the same FE80::/10 prefix exists on every interface the router needs the outgoing interface to know which link is meant.

caseStudies.title: Harbor Logistics: OSPF and Backup Routing
caseStudies.scenario: Harbor Logistics has a head office and a warehouse. At head office, three routers share one Ethernet segment, 10.0.0.0/24: HQ-A (router ID 1.1.1.1), HQ-B (2.2.2.2) and the Internet edge router Edge (3.3.3.3). All use OSPF area 0 with default timers, default OSPF priorities and the default reference bandwidth of 100 Mbps. The warehouse router W1 serves the LAN 172.16.1.0/24 through a Gigabit interface. W1 reaches HQ-A over a 10 Mbps Ethernet link and HQ-B over a 1.544 Mbps serial link. HQ-A and HQ-B use Gigabit on the head office segment. Edge has a static default route to the primary ISP and an additional static default route to an LTE backup, configured with administrative distance 150. The other routers must learn the default route dynamically from Edge, and the administrator also wants HQ-B to be the designated router on the head office segment.

questions.question: All three head office routers start at the same time with default priorities. Which router becomes the DR?
options: None; a DR is not elected on Ethernet
questions.explanation: With equal priorities, the highest router ID wins, and Edge (3.3.3.3) beats HQ-B (2.2.2.2) and HQ-A (1.1.1.1). HQ-B becomes the BDR. Ethernet is a broadcast network type, so the election does take place.

questions.question: What OSPF metric does HQ-A install for 172.16.1.0/24, assuming default costs and that HQ-A's outgoing interface toward W1 is its 10 Mbps Ethernet link?
questions.explanation: The metric is the sum of the outgoing interface costs along the best path: 10 for HQ-A's 10 Mbps link (100/10) plus 1 for W1's Gigabit LAN interface, 11 in all. The path through HQ-B would cost 1 + 64 + 1 = 66, and 10 forgets W1's LAN interface.

questions.question: Which command on Edge, in OSPF router configuration mode, makes the other routers learn the default route?
questions.explanation: default-information originate advertises Edge's default route into OSPF, where neighbors see it as an O*E2 route. A network statement with all zeros does not advertise a default, redistributing connected routes advertises subnets rather than a default, and passive-interface default would stop the adjacencies altogether.

questions.question: While the primary ISP default route is available, the LTE static default with administrative distance 150 is also installed in the routing table on Edge and carries half of the traffic.
questions.explanation: A floating static route with a higher AD than the primary stays out of the routing table and carries no traffic. It appears only when the better default route disappears.

caseStudies.title: Riverside Clinic: Securing the Network Edge
caseStudies.scenario: Riverside Clinic's edge router connects three internal networks: staff 192.168.10.0/24, a patient portal server network 192.168.20.0/24 and a guest Wi-Fi network 192.168.30.0/24. The router performs PAT for outbound traffic and publishes the portal server 192.168.20.10 at 203.0.113.10 using static NAT. Guests must reach the Internet but must never reach the staff or server networks. Last week a visitor plugged a home router into a wall port in the staff area; staff laptops briefly received addresses from it and lost connectivity. The IT contractor also administers the edge router and the switches over Telnet from an office PC, and the practice manager wants that replaced with something secure before a compliance review.

questions.question: Which ACL design best keeps the guests away from staff and server networks while still allowing Internet access?
options: An extended ACL on the guest gateway interface, inbound, denying the two internal networks and ending with permit ip any any
A standard ACL on the guest gateway interface, inbound, denying 192.168.30.0 0.0.0.255 as the source
An extended ACL ending with deny ip any any, applied outbound on the router WAN interface
An access-class on the vty lines that denies the guest subnet 192.168.30.0 0.0.0.255
questions.explanation: An extended ACL close to the source can name the destinations to block, and the final permit ip any any keeps Internet access working. A standard ACL would block guests from everything, including the Internet. An ACL at the WAN would be too far from the guests and a final deny would cut all traffic, while access-class only protects management sessions to the router itself.

questions.question: Which Layer 2 feature stops the visitor's home router from handing out addresses to staff laptops?
options: Dynamic ARP inspection enabled without DHCP snooping
Port security with a maximum of 5 MAC addresses per port
DHCP snooping with access ports untrusted and the uplink to the real server trusted
Static NAT on the edge router for the guest network
questions.explanation: DHCP snooping drops DHCP server messages that arrive on untrusted ports, so offers from the rogue device never reach clients. DAI depends on the snooping binding table and addresses ARP, port security counts MAC addresses and would not stop a single rogue DHCP server, and NAT does not operate at that layer.

questions.question: Which two steps are required to replace Telnet with SSH for administering the edge router? (Choose two.)
options: Generate an RSA key pair with crypto key generate rsa
Set transport input ssh on the vty lines
Configure ip helper-address on the management interface
Configure ntp master on the router
questions.explanation: The SSH server needs an RSA key pair, and the vty lines must be limited to SSH so Telnet is refused (along with a hostname, domain name and local user). A helper-address is for DHCP relay, service password-encryption only obfuscates stored passwords and NTP has nothing to do with enabling SSH.

compare.scenario: A company of 150 users in one building needs a campus design that is simple and affordable, with room for modest growth. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: A three-tier design with separate access, distribution and core switch pairs
compare.optionB: A two-tier design with access switches and a collapsed core and distribution layer
compare.why: A collapsed core delivers the needed redundancy and routing at far lower cost and complexity for a single building. The three-tier design is the tempting runner-up because it is the classic reference model, but its extra layer buys scalability that a 150-user site will not use.

compare.scenario: An organisation must link two floors with a run of about 150 metres in a conduit that runs past heavy electrical equipment. Which cabling is better?
compare.why: Copper Ethernet is limited to 100 metres per segment and is susceptible to electrical interference, while multimode fiber easily covers 150 metres and is immune to it. Cat6a is the tempting choice because it supports 10 Gbps, but the distance limit rules it out.

compare.scenario: A department needs a subnet for about 400 hosts today and expects no more than 450 in the next three years. Which allocation is better?
compare.why: A /23 covers the expected 450 hosts with room to spare and wastes the least address space. A /22 also works and is the tempting choice if you expect a lot more growth, but it reserves roughly double the space for needs that are not forecast.

compare.scenario: A campus distribution block has heavy traffic between VLANs on many access switches and needs wire-speed routing. Which inter-VLAN routing method is better?
compare.optionA: A router-on-a-stick with one trunk to the distribution switch
compare.optionB: Switch virtual interfaces on a layer 3 switch with ip routing enabled
compare.why: SVIs route in hardware at switch speeds and scale to many VLANs. Router-on-a-stick is the tempting runner-up because it is simple to configure, but all inter-VLAN traffic shares one link and the router's forwarding capacity.

compare.scenario: A network of Cisco switches runs per-VLAN spanning tree and users complain that after a link failure the network is down for almost a minute. Which change is better?
compare.optionA: Lower the hello timer to 1 second on every switch
compare.optionB: Enable Rapid PVST+ with spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
compare.why: Rapid PVST+ negotiates topology changes with neighbours and converges in seconds. Tuning timers on classic PVST+ is the tempting alternative, but it is fragile and still bound by max age and the listening and learning states.

compare.scenario: A switch must form an EtherChannel with a firewall from another vendor. Which negotiation choice is better?
compare.why: LACP is the IEEE standard and is understood by multi-vendor equipment. PAgP is Cisco-proprietary and is the tempting answer only because the switch is a Cisco device; the far end would not understand it.

compare.scenario: An enterprise headquarters has a high-speed local controller and wants all wireless client traffic to pass through the controller for central policy enforcement. Which AP mode is better?
compare.optionA: Local mode with CAPWAP tunnels to the WLC
compare.why: Local mode tunnels all client traffic to the controller, giving the central inspection the scenario asks for. FlexConnect is the tempting runner-up because it is flexible, but locally switched traffic bypasses the controller and is intended for branch sites with remote controllers.

compare.scenario: A team needs to push the same configuration to 30 routers that cannot run any extra agent software, using human-readable playbooks. Which tool is better?
compare.optionA: Puppet, with an agent on every router
compare.optionB: Ansible, pushing YAML playbooks over SSH
compare.why: Ansible is agentless and uses YAML playbooks over SSH or APIs, so the routers need no extra software. Puppet is the tempting answer because it is also a configuration management tool, but its typical agent-based design does not fit devices that cannot host agents.

compare.scenario: A branch has an OSPF-learned default route from headquarters (AD 110) and a second ISP link. The engineer wants the second link used ONLY if the OSPF default is lost. Which configuration is better?
compare.why: The floating static route with AD 150 is less trusted than the OSPF default at 110, so it stays hidden until OSPF fails. The default static route at AD 1 is the tempting runner-up because it is simpler, but it is more trusted than OSPF and would replace the primary path immediately.

compare.scenario: A distribution layer runs routers from two different vendors. Both must serve as redundant default gateway for the same VLAN with one virtual IP. Which protocol is better?
compare.optionA: HSRP, which is widely deployed and simple to configure
compare.optionB: VRRP, which is defined by an open standard
compare.why: VRRP works across vendors because it is an IETF standard. HSRP is the tempting runner-up since it is familiar to Cisco engineers, but it is proprietary, so the non-Cisco router could not join the group.

compare.scenario: Two routers are connected by a dedicated Ethernet link with no other devices. Which OSPF setup on that link is better?
compare.optionA: Leave the default broadcast network type and let the routers elect a DR and BDR
compare.optionB: Configure ip ospf network point-to-point on both interfaces
compare.why: With only two routers, a DR election adds delay and a pointless role; point-to-point skips the election and goes straight to Full. The default is the tempting runner-up because it works, but it adds the election wait and DR concepts that serve no purpose on a two-router link.

compare.scenario: A company with 300 internal hosts has a single public IPv4 address from its ISP and needs all hosts to browse the Internet at the same time. Which is better?
compare.optionA: Dynamic NAT with a pool containing the one public address
compare.optionB: PAT, with ip nat inside source list ... interface ... overload
compare.why: PAT multiplexes hundreds of hosts onto one address using port numbers. Dynamic NAT with a pool of one address is the tempting runner-up, but it maps hosts one-to-one, so only a single host could be translated at a time.

compare.scenario: On a congested WAN link, voice calls suffer delay and jitter while bulk backups run. Which tool best fixes the voice quality problem?
compare.optionA: Weighted random early detection on the WAN interface
compare.optionB: Low-latency queuing with voice marked EF in a strict priority queue
compare.why: A strict priority queue lets voice packets leave first, removing queuing delay and jitter. WRED is the tempting runner-up because it deals with congestion, but it drops packets early to slow TCP senders and does not give voice any priority.

compare.scenario: A company wants engineers authenticated centrally and each command they type authorized and logged. Which AAA protocol is better?
compare.why: TACACS+ keeps authentication, authorization and accounting separate, so individual commands can be authorized and recorded. RADIUS is the tempting runner-up because it is an open, widely supported standard, but it merges authentication with authorization and is better suited to network access such as Wi-Fi and 802.1X.

compare.scenario: Users report wrong gateway addresses because someone connected a small router running DHCP to an access port. Which switch feature is the better fix?
compare.optionA: Port security with maximum 1 MAC address per port
compare.optionB: DHCP snooping, trusting only the uplink to the legitimate server
compare.why: DHCP snooping drops server messages on untrusted ports, which is exactly the rogue-server problem. Port security is the tempting runner-up because it also protects the access edge, but one device running a DHCP server uses only one MAC address and passes the check.

compare.scenario: A company has 500 employees on Wi-Fi and must remove a departing employee's access immediately without disturbing anyone else. Which design is better?
compare.optionB: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X and a RADIUS server
compare.why: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually, so one account can be disabled instantly. WPA3-Personal is the tempting runner-up because it is newer and stronger against guessing, but a shared passphrase cannot be revoked per person without changing it for everyone.
